content_html:
Credit card interest is charged on whatever balance you carry from month to month, and at typical card rates it adds up quickly. This calculator shows how long a fixed monthly payment takes to clear a balance and how much interest you pay along the way, or, if you have a target date in mind, the monthly payment that gets you there.

How to use this calculator

  1. Current balance: the amount you owe today, from your latest statement or online account.
  2. Interest rate (APR): the annual percentage rate on purchases. If part of the balance is on a promotional rate, use the rate that applies to most of it.
  3. What do you want to work out: choose a fixed monthly payment to see how long payoff takes, or a number of months to see the payment you need.
  4. More options: add any new charges you expect to keep making each month and the card's annual fee, if it has one.

The results show the payoff time or the required payment, the total interest, the total of all payments and the month you would make your final payment. The schedule lists every month so you can see the balance fall.

How the payoff is calculated

Each month the calculator divides the APR by 12 and charges that rate on the balance. It then adds any new charges, adds the annual fee every twelfth month, and subtracts your payment. This repeats until the balance reaches zero. The last payment is usually smaller because it only needs to cover what is left.

With no new charges, the number of months has a closed form: n = −ln(1 − r × B / P) / ln(1 + r), where B is the balance, P the payment and r the monthly rate. To find the payment for a set number of months, it searches for the smallest payment, to the cent, that clears the balance in time. If your payment does not cover the first month's interest and new charges, the balance never goes down and the calculator tells you so.

A worked example

Suppose you owe $5,000 at 22% APR and pay $150 a month. The first month's interest is about $91.67, so only around $58 of the first payment reduces the balance. The card is paid off in 52 payments (4 years 4 months), and the interest comes to $2,798.05, meaning you pay $7,798.05 in total.

Monthly paymentTime to pay offTotal interest

$2502 years 2 months$1,285.72

To be debt-free in 36 months instead, the payment rises to $190.96 and total interest falls to $1,874.17. The jump from $100 to $150 a month saves more than $5,800, which is why even a modest increase makes such a difference at card rates.

Tips for paying down a card faster

  • Pay a fixed amount, not the minimum. Minimum payments shrink as the balance falls, which stretches repayment out for years. Keeping the payment fixed shortens payoff dramatically.
  • Stop adding to the balance. Use the new charges field to see how ongoing spending slows your progress.
  • Ask about a lower rate. Try a lower APR in the calculator to see what a rate reduction or a balance transfer could save, then weigh it against any transfer fee.
  • Target the highest rate first. If you have several cards, extra money goes furthest on the one with the highest APR.

Results are estimates. Card issuers calculate interest on the average daily balance, and rates can change, so your statements may differ slightly from the schedule.

faq.question: Why does my balance go down so slowly at first?
faq.answer: Early in repayment, a large share of each payment goes to interest because the balance is at its highest. As the balance falls, the interest charge shrinks and more of each payment reduces what you owe.

faq.question: What happens if I only pay the minimum?
faq.answer: The minimum payment is usually a small percentage of the balance plus interest, so it drops as the balance drops. That keeps the debt around much longer and greatly increases the total interest compared with paying a fixed amount.

faq.question: Does paying more than once a month help?
faq.answer: It can help a little. Card interest accrues daily on the balance, so paying earlier in the cycle lowers the average balance and trims the interest charge. The bigger factor is the total amount you pay each month.

faq.question: Should I include the annual fee?
faq.answer: Include it if you plan to keep the card open while paying it off and the fee is charged to the card. It is added to the balance every 12 months in this calculator.

faq.question: Is my information stored or sent anywhere?
faq.answer: No. The calculation runs entirely in your browser, and nothing you enter is sent to a server or saved.
